title: How to Build a College List Before Winter Break
summary: Build a balanced college list before winter break with an IB-focused September-November plan covering fit, predicted grades, costs, and deadlines.
body_markdown:
If you want to **build a college list before winter break** , finish broad research by late October and approve a final, affordable list by the end of November. IB students should check course prerequisites, Higher Level requirements, predicted-grade expectations, costs, deadlines, and application workload, not just reputation or general admission rates.


Completing this work during the **IB uniapp fall term** protects December for essays, application checks, and IB revision. The aim is a balanced set of universities for which you are academically eligible, financially prepared, and genuinely interested in attending.


### What a finished college list should contain


A college list is not simply a collection of institutions you like. Every option should be academically possible, financially workable, and suitable for the subject and university experience you want.


For US applicants, approximately **8-12 final applications** is often manageable, although there is no official ideal. UCAS permits up to **five choices** , so students applying internationally should not force every system into a US-style model.


A strong list includes:


- Courses for which you meet all required IB subject and level conditions
- A balance of ambitious, realistic, and more secure options
- At least two affordable institutions you would be happy to attend
- Verified application, scholarship, testing, and portfolio deadlines
- A manageable number of essays and supplementary tasks
- Alternatives if your final IB results differ from your prediction


Admission is never guaranteed, so **likely** is more accurate than “safety.” A university can be academically likely but financially unrealistic, while a generally accessible institution may be highly selective for a particular programme.


### Start with the course, not the university name


Define what you want to study before comparing institutions. Course content, assessment, professional accreditation, and subject prerequisites usually matter more than a university’s overall ranking.


For each course, investigate:


- Required or preferred **HL subjects**
- Minimum total IB score and required HL grades
- Mathematics requirements, especially **Analysis and Approaches** versus **Applications and Interpretation**
- Admissions tests, interviews, auditions, or portfolios
- Compulsory modules, placements, research options, and flexibility
- Accreditation required for professional practice


Requirements often belong to the individual programme rather than the institution, as explained in RevisionDojo’s guide to[IB minimum scores by university](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-minimum-score-by-university) . Use the[official IB university recognition database](https://recognition.ibo.org/en-US/) for initial research, but confirm current conditions on each university’s official course page. An IB recognition statement does not guarantee admission.


### Build a comparison spreadsheet


Create one row per course and record the date on which you checked each source. Requirements can change between admission cycles, so preserve official links rather than relying on memory.


Category What to record


Academic entry IB total, HL profile, required subjects, English requirements


Predicted grades Current prediction and its position against stated conditions


Application plan Early Decision, Early Action, Regular Decision, UCAS, or direct


Deadlines University, school, aid, testing, and portfolio dates


Course fit Modules, teaching style, flexibility, placements, research


Personal fit Location, size, housing, campus, and student support


Financial fit Net price, scholarships, travel, visa, and living costs


Workload Essays, recommendations, interviews, and portfolio tasks


Status Researching, keep, remove, or final


Set non-negotiable criteria before comparing universities. These might include a maximum annual cost, required engineering accreditation, clinical placements, or a particular location. This prevents prestige from overriding factors that will shape your education and daily life.


### Interpret your IB profile realistically


Use your current transcript, school-approved predicted grades, HL subjects, and school context. Do not convert an IB score into a GPA unless a university explicitly requests it. RevisionDojo’s guide to[reporting the IB in US college applications](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-in-college-apps-us) explains how courses, levels, school records, and predictions commonly appear.


Classify each option carefully:


- **Ambitious:** You meet the requirements, but selection is highly competitive or your profile is near the lower end.
- **Realistic:** Your grades align with published expectations and you satisfy every prerequisite.
- **More secure:** You are comfortably above stated conditions and the programme is less selective, without assuming guaranteed admission.


Published minimums are not always competitive levels. A course requiring 36 points may admit many students with higher predictions. US institutions using holistic review may publish no fixed IB cutoff, so grades, rigor, recommendations, activities, and essays must be considered together.


Ask your counsellor when approved predictions become available and which documents universities receive.[Predicted-grade submission timing](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/when-are-ib-predicted-grades-submitted-to-universities-what-every-student-needs-to-know) varies by school and application system.


### Treat affordability as an admission condition


A university is not realistic if your family cannot fund it under plausible aid scenarios. Compare **net price** , not only tuition or advertised cost of attendance. Loans reduce the immediate price but still require repayment.


For US institutions, use each college’s calculator and consult[Federal Student Aid guidance on choosing a school](https://studentaid.gov/resources/prepare-for-college/students/choosing-schools) . Check whether scholarships require separate applications, earlier deadlines, interviews, or essays. International applicants should verify aid eligibility and whether requesting aid affects admission.


Discuss an affordable maximum before considering binding Early Decision. If comparing financial offers is essential, a non-binding application route may offer greater flexibility.


### Follow a September-November schedule


### September: create the longlist


Begin with approximately **15-20 possibilities** . Define your subject, cost, location, and campus preferences; identify prerequisites; confirm predicted-grade timing; and enter university and internal school deadlines into one calendar. Ask recommenders early and follow your school’s procedure.


Students applying across countries should maintain separate deadline columns. RevisionDojo’s[global IB university application guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-apply-to-university-as-an-ib-student-step-by-step-guide-for-global-admissions) explains how systems and documentation differ.


### October: test academic and financial fit


Reduce the longlist by comparing your profile with official requirements, reviewing course content, and calculating likely costs. Attend open days or virtual sessions where useful.


For **2027 UCAS entry** , the deadline is **15 October 2026 at 18:00 UK time** for Oxford, Cambridge, and most medicine, dentistry, and veterinary medicine or science courses. Most other undergraduate courses have an equal-consideration deadline of **13 January 2027 at 18:00 UK time** . Confirm dates on the[official UCAS deadline page](https://www.ucas.com/applying/applying-to-university/dates-and-deadlines-for-uni-applications) , and remember that schools often set earlier internal deadlines.


US colleges set their own dates. Check the[Common App requirements resources](https://www.commonapp.org/apply/fy-toolkit/) and each institution’s admission page rather than using a generic calendar.


### November: approve the final list


Every remaining course should pass four tests: you meet its prerequisites, it suits your goals, its estimated cost is manageable, and you can complete the application on time. Finish November with a final spreadsheet, essay inventory, and submission calendar.


Continue preparing regular-decision applications after an early submission unless a binding result resolves your plans. This prevents a deferral or rejection from forcing you to rebuild the list during winter break.


### Common mistakes to avoid


- **Choosing by prestige alone:** Reputation cannot fix an unsuitable course, missing prerequisite, or unaffordable cost.
- **Treating every lower-ranked institution as safe:** Selectivity varies by programme, residency, and applicant category.
- **Using unofficial summaries:** Requirements can become outdated, so verify official course pages.
- **Ignoring school deadlines:** Counsellors need time for transcripts, references, and predictions.
- **Waiting for a higher prediction:** Research using current evidence, then adjust after an approved change. The guide to[predicted grades versus final scores](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/should-i-apply-to-college-with-predicted-grades-or-wait-for-final-scores-a-complete-ib-guide) explains the distinction.
- **Applying to too many institutions:** Extra applications add research, fees, writing, and administration.


### Final pre-break checklist


Before winter break, confirm that every course meets your criteria, your list includes varied levels of selectivity, and at least two options are affordable and appealing. Copy deadlines from official sources, confirm document arrangements with your counsellor, schedule every supplementary task, and retain a backup plan for an early deferral or rejection.


The objective is not the longest list. It is a researched set of universities that you can afford, qualify for, and willingly attend. RevisionDojo Study Notes, Questionbank practice, Jojo AI, and the Grade Predictor can help you protect your IB performance while applications are underway.
